questions.q: Why does each Dockerfile use a multi-stage build?
options: To make the Dockerfile shorter
So the final runtime image doesn't carry build tools, dev dependencies, or install caches from the build stage
Because Docker requires at least two FROM statements
To allow the image to run on both Linux and Windows
questions.explain: Multi-stage builds let a build stage install dependencies and compile artifacts, then a separate runtime stage copies only what's needed — keeping build tools and caches out of the image that actually ships.

questions.q: What does the `USER app` instruction accomplish in both Dockerfiles?
options: It names the container for logging purposes
It switches the running process to a non-root, unprivileged user
It creates a new Docker volume called app
It sets the application's display name in the UI
questions.explain: USER app switches the container's process to a non-root user created earlier in the Dockerfile, so the application never runs as root inside the container.

questions.q: What is the image tagging convention used throughout this capstone?
options: northbridgeacr.azurecr.io/<service>:latest
northbridgeacr.azurecr.io/<service>:<git-sha>
A random UUID generated at build time
The developer's username and the current date
questions.explain: Every image is tagged with the git SHA of the commit that produced it — e.g. northbridgeacr.azurecr.io/checkout:a1b2c3d — never latest, so every running image is traceable to an exact commit.

questions.q: Which file type is most important to exclude via `.dockerignore`, and why?
options: `.md` files, because they make the image too large
`.env`, because it can contain local secrets that should never be baked into an image layer
`Dockerfile` itself, because Docker refuses to build otherwise
`package.json`, because npm ignores it anyway
questions.explain: .env holds local secrets such as the PaymentPro sandbox key. Keeping it out of the build context via .dockerignore prevents it from ever being baked into an image layer.

questions.q: What practical benefit does SHA-based image tagging give the team once Trivy scanning and CI are added in Chapter 4?
options: It makes builds run faster
It lets anyone trace a running image back to the exact commit that produced it, which matters for debugging and postmortems
It automatically fixes any CRITICAL vulnerabilities Trivy finds
It removes the need for a container registry entirely
questions.explain: SHA tagging gives full traceability from a running image back to its source commit — essential when debugging a rollback or writing a postmortem after an incident.
